Background
The microbiota composition of the human gut changes
with age, and alterations in this composition influence
human health.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
In the early 1970s, culture-based methods
were used to demonstrate that the gut microbiota
composition changes during the aging process [1].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Re-
cent studies using molecular methods have also indicated
clear differences in the composition of gut microbiota
among infants, toddlers, adults and the elderly [2].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
It has been recently
shown that the gut microbiota is not yet established
at 5 years of age [11].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
However,
almost all studies related to the gut microbiota of the
elderly have been performed on subjects classified
into segmented age groups based on varying defini-
tions of ‘elderly’, such as ‘over 60’ [12], ‘over 65’ [13],
‘over 70’ [14] or ‘centenarian’ [15].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Fur-
thermore, although abundant data on gut microbiota
composition are available in some public databases,
sequential changes cannot be evaluated with these
public data because of biases stemming from differ-
ences in study methods, especially in DNA extraction
[16, 17], and nationality differences among the sub-
jects [9, 18–22].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Our results provide new insights
into the developmental period for gut microbiota
composition and the patterns of change with age.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Claesson et al. re-
ported that the alpha diversity of the gut microbiota in
community dwellers was significantly higher than that of
people in long-stay care [42].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
In contrast, centenarians in
a Chinese longevous village population had a more
diverse gut microbiota than did younger elderly aged
85–99 years [43].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Biagi et al. [44] showed a significantly compromised
gut microbiota in centenarians but not in elderly sub-
jects aged approximately 70 years compared with a
group of younger adults.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
The authors therefore sug-
gested that a healthy gut microbiota community might
be affected by aging-related physiological and behavioral
changes that occur after 70 years of age, which was con-
sidered the threshold age for defining an individual as
elderly.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
This result
suggested that other factors besides age contribute to
the composition of gut microbiota communities.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
To begin
to address this question, we performed PICRUSt analysis
to predict the relative abundance of transporter genes
because we hypothesized that bacterial transporters that
incorporate nutrients from the gut environment would
differ if dietary habit was a predominant contributor to
gut microbiota composition.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Therefore, the decline in gastrointestinal tract func-
tionality in the elderly may also lead to significant changes
in gut microbiota.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Conclusion
In conclusion, we provide a description of the changes
in gut microbiota with age, thus illustrating the long tra-
jectory throughout human life.

Results
Overview of gut microbiota composition in each age
group
A total of 1,839,703 high-quality paired sequences were
obtained from the 371 samples, with 4,959 ± 1,813
(average ± standard deviation) reads per sample, which
were clustered into 5,952 OTUs and classified into 187
bacterial groups at the genus level (186 genera and one
unidentified
group).

Furthermore, our
results showed that Japanese adults (21–69 years old)
have a greater abundance of the genera Blautia and
Bifidobacterium (interquartile ranges (IQR) of 18 (12–24)
% and 7 (2–14) %, respectively) and a relatively lower
abundance of genera related to Bacteroidetes (IQR 4
(1–10) %), compared with those reported in previous
studies in other nations.

raw_entities.context:

shown that the gut microbiota is not yet established

almost all studies related to the gut microbiota of the

‘over 70’ [14] or ‘centenarian’ [15].

and how the microbiota composition shifts from the
adult stage to the elderly stage.

In conclusion, we provide a description of the changes

Background
The microbiota composition of the human gut changes
with age, and alterations in this composition influence
human health.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
In the early 1970s, culture-based methods
were used to demonstrate that the gut microbiota
composition changes during the aging process [1].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Re-
cent studies using molecular methods have also indicated
clear differences in the composition of gut microbiota
among infants, toddlers, adults and the elderly [2].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
It has been recently
shown that the gut microbiota is not yet established
at 5 years of age [11].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
However,
almost all studies related to the gut microbiota of the
elderly have been performed on subjects classified
into segmented age groups based on varying defini-
tions of ‘elderly’, such as ‘over 60’ [12], ‘over 65’ [13],
‘over 70’ [14] or ‘centenarian’ [15].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Fur-
thermore, although abundant data on gut microbiota
composition are available in some public databases,
sequential changes cannot be evaluated with these
public data because of biases stemming from differ-
ences in study methods, especially in DNA extraction
[16, 17], and nationality differences among the sub-
jects [9, 18–22].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Our results provide new insights
into the developmental period for gut microbiota
composition and the patterns of change with age.

clarify the relationships among gut microbiota.

In addition, a low
gut microbiota diversity has been associated with an
increasing number of conditions, such as autism [38],
autoimmune disease [39] and obesity [40].

Maintaining
sufficient bacterial richness and diversity is important
for providing gut microbiota with functional redun-

and
thus
systematic
robustness
against environmental challenges [41].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY

In this study, we
observed an increase in gut microbiota diversity with
aging until the centenarian stage.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Claesson et al. re-
ported that the alpha diversity of the gut microbiota in
community dwellers was significantly higher than that of
people in long-stay care [42].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
In contrast, centenarians in
a Chinese longevous village population had a more
diverse gut microbiota than did younger elderly aged
85–99 years [43].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Biagi et al. [44] showed a significantly compromised
gut microbiota in centenarians but not in elderly sub-
jects aged approximately 70 years compared with a
group of younger adults.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
The authors therefore sug-
gested that a healthy gut microbiota community might
be affected by aging-related physiological and behavioral
changes that occur after 70 years of age, which was con-
sidered the threshold age for defining an individual as
elderly.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
This result
suggested that other factors besides age contribute to
the composition of gut microbiota communities.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
To begin
to address this question, we performed PICRUSt analysis
to predict the relative abundance of transporter genes
because we hypothesized that bacterial transporters that
incorporate nutrients from the gut environment would
differ if dietary habit was a predominant contributor to
gut microbiota composition.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Therefore, the decline in gastrointestinal tract func-
tionality in the elderly may also lead to significant changes
in gut microbiota.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Conclusion
In conclusion, we provide a description of the changes
in gut microbiota with age, thus illustrating the long tra-
jectory throughout human life.

some patterns and transition points in gut microbiota
composition with age.

group).

results showed that Japanese adults (21–69 years old)
have a greater abundance of the genera Blautia and

% and 7 (2–14) %, respectively) and a relatively lower
abundance of genera related to Bacteroidetes (IQR 4
(1–10) %), compared with those reported in previous
studies in other nations.

Background
The microbiota composition of the human gut changes
with age, and alterations in this composition influence
human health.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
In the early 1970s, culture-based methods
were used to demonstrate that the gut microbiota
composition changes during the aging process [1].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
After
birth, the initial microbiota composition is affected by the
mode of birth [3–5] and the mother’s gut microbiota
[6, 7].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
A recent report
suggested that the age-affiliated microbiota population
shifts from 3 days to 2 years after birth and that major
differences are apparent between 2 years and adulthood
[8].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
It has been recently
shown that the gut microbiota is not yet established
at 5 years of age [11].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
However,
almost all studies related to the gut microbiota of the
elderly have been performed on subjects classified
into segmented age groups based on varying defini-
tions of ‘elderly’, such as ‘over 60’ [12], ‘over 65’ [13],
‘over 70’ [14] or ‘centenarian’ [15].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
It is unclear when
and how the microbiota composition shifts from the
adult stage to the elderly stage.

Discussion
The composition of gut microbiota is thought to change
during the aging process [1]; however, few reports have
utilized molecular techniques to investigate the long-
term, sequential changes in gut microbiota composition.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Our results are in agreement with those of recent studies
indicating clear differences in gut microbiota compos-
ition among infants, adults and the elderly [2, 23].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
These patterns might be characteristic of
the gut microbiota composition of the Japanese popu-
lation,
although
they
may
also
reflect
the
DNA
extraction method [16, 17] and the amplified region
of the 16S rRNA gene [24].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Although there are differences among individuals, our
analysis of the phylum composition of gut microbiota in
each age group showed a significant shift in the relative
abundance of Actinobacteria in infants from before to
after weaning.

Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium CAGs and the

reflecting the human gut microbiota maturation process.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI

Each
number below the figure indicates a group as shown in Table 1

Page 5 of 12
Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium CAGs and the
alpha diversity of gut microbiota continued to change
sequentially with age in subjects younger than twenty,
reflecting the human gut microbiota maturation process.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
However, children younger than 20 years fell into both
the infant and adult clusters, regardless of their age,
when clustered based on the abundance of genus-like
groups, thus illustrating the individual differences in the
gut microbiota maturation process.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Considering these
reports, the correlations between gut microbiota mem-
bers might be more complicated than shown in the Wig-
gum plot.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
In addition, a low
gut microbiota diversity has been associated with an
increasing number of conditions, such as autism [38],
autoimmune disease [39] and obesity [40].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Maintaining
sufficient bacterial richness and diversity is important
for providing gut microbiota with functional redun-
dancy,
adaptability
and
thus
systematic
robustness
against environmental challenges [41].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
In this study, we
observed an increase in gut microbiota diversity with
aging until the centenarian stage.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Claesson et al. re-
ported that the alpha diversity of the gut microbiota in
community dwellers was significantly higher than that of
people in long-stay care [42].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
Biagi et al. [44] showed a significantly compromised
gut microbiota in centenarians but not in elderly sub-
jects aged approximately 70 years compared with a
group of younger adults.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
The authors therefore sug-
gested that a healthy gut microbiota community might
be affected by aging-related physiological and behavioral
changes that occur after 70 years of age, which was con-
sidered the threshold age for defining an individual as
elderly.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
To begin
to address this question, we performed PICRUSt analysis
to predict the relative abundance of transporter genes
because we hypothesized that bacterial transporters that
incorporate nutrients from the gut environment would
differ if dietary habit was a predominant contributor to
gut microbiota composition.

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
In addition, elderly people are known to have decreased
intestinal function relative to younger people, which
affects digestion, nutrient absorption and immune activity
[45, 46] and may also impact the microbiota composition
[47, 48].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Conclusion
In conclusion, we provide a description of the changes
in gut microbiota with age, thus illustrating the long tra-
jectory throughout human life.

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
The gut microbiota in subjects
younger than 20 years changed with age as it matured,
and that of subjects older than 70 years changed again
into
the
elderly
type.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
In
addition,
the
transporter
property prediction results suggested that nutrients in
the gut might play an important role in changing the gut
microbiota composition with age.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Our findings help clarify the gut microbiota compos-
ition in a healthy population at each age period.

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
Further
analyses investigating lifestyle traits or prospective co-
horts focused on subjects who appear to have a gut
microbiota typical of an age group older than their
matched
age
would
be
valuable
for
revealing
the
relationships between gut microbiota and host health,
including the aging process.

Background
The microbiota composition of the human gut changes
with age, and alterations in this composition influence
human health.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
In the early 1970s, culture-based methods
were used to demonstrate that the gut microbiota
composition changes during the aging process [1].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Re-
cent studies using molecular methods have also indicated
clear differences in the composition of gut microbiota
among infants, toddlers, adults and the elderly [2].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
It has been recently
shown that the gut microbiota is not yet established
at 5 years of age [11].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
However,
almost all studies related to the gut microbiota of the
elderly have been performed on subjects classified
into segmented age groups based on varying defini-
tions of ‘elderly’, such as ‘over 60’ [12], ‘over 65’ [13],
‘over 70’ [14] or ‘centenarian’ [15].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Fur-
thermore, although abundant data on gut microbiota
composition are available in some public databases,
sequential changes cannot be evaluated with these
public data because of biases stemming from differ-
ences in study methods, especially in DNA extraction
[16, 17], and nationality differences among the sub-
jects [9, 18–22].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Our results provide new insights
into the developmental period for gut microbiota
composition and the patterns of change with age.

Discussion
The composition of gut microbiota is thought to change
during the aging process [1]; however, few reports have
utilized molecular techniques to investigate the long-
term, sequential changes in gut microbiota composition.

Our results are in agreement with those of recent studies
indicating clear differences in gut microbiota compos-

increasing number of conditions, such as autism [38],
autoimmune disease [39] and obesity [40].

and

raw_entities.label: ENTITY

Claesson et al. re-
ported that the alpha diversity of the gut microbiota in
community dwellers was significantly higher than that of
people in long-stay care [42].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
In contrast, centenarians in
a Chinese longevous village population had a more
diverse gut microbiota than did younger elderly aged
85–99 years [43].

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Biagi et al. [44] showed a significantly compromised
gut microbiota in centenarians but not in elderly sub-
jects aged approximately 70 years compared with a
group of younger adults.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
The authors therefore sug-
gested that a healthy gut microbiota community might
be affected by aging-related physiological and behavioral
changes that occur after 70 years of age, which was con-
sidered the threshold age for defining an individual as
elderly.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
This result
suggested that other factors besides age contribute to
the composition of gut microbiota communities.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
To begin
to address this question, we performed PICRUSt analysis
to predict the relative abundance of transporter genes
because we hypothesized that bacterial transporters that
incorporate nutrients from the gut environment would
differ if dietary habit was a predominant contributor to
gut microbiota composition.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY
raw_entities.context:
Therefore, the decline in gastrointestinal tract func-
tionality in the elderly may also lead to significant changes
in gut microbiota.

raw_entities.label: ENTITY

Conclusion
In conclusion, we provide a description of the changes
in gut microbiota with age, thus illustrating the long tra-
jectory throughout human life.

Background
The microbiota composition of the human gut changes
with age, and alterations in this composition influence
human health.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
In the early 1970s, culture-based methods
were used to demonstrate that the gut microbiota
composition changes during the aging process [1].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
After
birth, the initial microbiota composition is affected by the
mode of birth [3–5] and the mother’s gut microbiota
[6, 7].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
A recent report
suggested that the age-affiliated microbiota population
shifts from 3 days to 2 years after birth and that major
differences are apparent between 2 years and adulthood
[8].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
It has been recently
shown that the gut microbiota is not yet established
at 5 years of age [11].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
However,
almost all studies related to the gut microbiota of the
elderly have been performed on subjects classified
into segmented age groups based on varying defini-
tions of ‘elderly’, such as ‘over 60’ [12], ‘over 65’ [13],
‘over 70’ [14] or ‘centenarian’ [15].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
It is unclear when
and how the microbiota composition shifts from the
adult stage to the elderly stage.

The composition of gut microbiota is thought to change
during the aging process [1]; however, few reports have
utilized molecular techniques to investigate the long-

Our results are in agreement with those of recent studies
indicating clear differences in gut microbiota compos-

each age group showed a significant shift in the relative

after weaning.

However, children younger than 20 years fell into both

when clustered based on the abundance of genus-like

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Considering these
reports, the correlations between gut microbiota mem-
bers might be more complicated than shown in the Wig-
gum plot.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
In addition, a low
gut microbiota diversity has been associated with an
increasing number of conditions, such as autism [38],
autoimmune disease [39] and obesity [40].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Maintaining
sufficient bacterial richness and diversity is important
for providing gut microbiota with functional redun-
dancy,
adaptability
and
thus
systematic
robustness
against environmental challenges [41].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
In this study, we
observed an increase in gut microbiota diversity with
aging until the centenarian stage.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Claesson et al. re-
ported that the alpha diversity of the gut microbiota in
community dwellers was significantly higher than that of
people in long-stay care [42].

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
Biagi et al. [44] showed a significantly compromised
gut microbiota in centenarians but not in elderly sub-
jects aged approximately 70 years compared with a
group of younger adults.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
The authors therefore sug-
gested that a healthy gut microbiota community might
be affected by aging-related physiological and behavioral
changes that occur after 70 years of age, which was con-
sidered the threshold age for defining an individual as
elderly.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
To begin
to address this question, we performed PICRUSt analysis
to predict the relative abundance of transporter genes
because we hypothesized that bacterial transporters that
incorporate nutrients from the gut environment would
differ if dietary habit was a predominant contributor to
gut microbiota composition.

raw_entities.label: TAXON
raw_entities.context:
In addition, elderly people are known to have decreased
intestinal function relative to younger people, which
affects digestion, nutrient absorption and immune activity
[45, 46] and may also impact the microbiota composition
[47, 48].

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Conclusion
In conclusion, we provide a description of the changes
in gut microbiota with age, thus illustrating the long tra-
jectory throughout human life.

younger than 20 years changed with age as it matured,
and that of subjects older than 70 years changed again
into
the
elderly
type.

In
addition,
the
transporter
property prediction results suggested that nutrients in
the gut might play an important role in changing the gut
microbiota composition with age.

raw_entities.label: CHEBI
raw_entities.context:
Our findings help clarify the gut microbiota compos-
ition in a healthy population at each age period.

microbiota typical of an age group older than their
matched

for

relationships between gut microbiota and host health,
